The thread, which has already amassed some four hundred replies within hours, betrays a forum evenly split between those who champion crypto's asymmetric upside and those who, scarred by prior drawdowns, treat the yellow metal as the only rational hedge against monetary debasement. clips.text_en_c2: Bitcoin versus gold: a perennial dilemma reframed for the coming decade. An anonymous poster on /biz/ posed the question this morning, asking which asset one ought to hold exclusively for the next ten years, and by what rationale. Within hours the thread had ballooned past four hundred replies, a microcosm of speculative conviction and bruised hindsight. Commentators cite gold's millennia-long store-of-value pedigree against Bitcoin's volatility and untested monetary thesis. Several anons confess to having lost money on both, though gold remains, for them, a sort of financial trauma from which recovery seems improbable. The discussion, predictably, devolves into tribal allegiance, with each camp dismissing the other as deluded. The underlying question, of course, remains unanswered, as it has been for every generation of retail investors who mistook optimism for analysis.

clips.text_zh: 肥仔信睇到呢條應該又笑我😅220kg double⋯我都未摸過桿。考牌都未搞掂，gym真係冇時間🧐
clips.text_en_b1: I went deadlifting again, I did 220 kg for a double. I thought I could do more reps, I think I'm just good at single reps, I'm not good at higher reps. My PR is 240 kg and I have gotten stronger since. This is my first time deadlifting in over a month.
clips.text_en_b2: I dragged myself back to the deadlift platform today and pulled 220 kilograms for a clean double, although honestly I thought I had at least one more rep in the tank. I seem to be built for heavy singles rather than grinding out high-volume sets, which is a bit frustrating. My all-time PR is still 240 kilograms, but since then I have gradually put on strength, so knocking that out feels within reach.
clips.text_en_c1: After an absence of more than four weeks from any serious pulling work, I returned to the platform today and managed a clean double at 220 kilograms, although I had quietly anticipated a third repetition that simply refused to materialise. The pattern is becoming familiar: for whatever reason, my nervous system seems primed for heavy singles rather than the grinding endurance demanded by higher rep ranges, a peculiarity that makes programming somewhat frustrating. My previous personal record sits at 240 kilograms, and given the strength gains accumulated since, surpassing that figure feels less like a question of if than when.
clips.text_en_c2: Returning to the platform after a layoff of more than a month, I managed a 220 kilogram double on the deadlift, a figure that, while respectable, fell short of the ambitions I had harboured upon warming up. I had genuinely expected to grind out additional repetitions; my physiology, it seems, is better suited to single maximal efforts than to higher-volume work, a peculiar asymmetry I have only recently begun to appreciate. Since recording my previous personal record of 240 kilograms, I have continued to add mass to my frame and refine my technique, though rust inevitably accumulates during extended absence. The session reaffirmed what I already suspected: strength, once banked, demands continual maintenance, and the barbell, unforgiving as ever, remembers nothing of past feats.

clips.text_en_c1: Anyone harbouring fantasies of snapping up Nvidia hardware at clearance prices once the artificial intelligence bubble eventually deflates should disabuse themselves of the notion rather swiftly, because the prevailing rumour, posted this morning on /g/, suggests that once hyperscale operators finish purchasing, the remaining stock will simply be smelted into raw silicon. The thread has ignited considerable debate regarding whether consumer-grade GPUs retain any meaningful resale value whatsoever in a market where the principal buyer, the data centre complex, abruptly withdraws its bids. Engineers whose livelihoods depend on the ecosystem watch nervously from the sidelines.
clips.text_en_c2: The notion that GPUs will become affordable once the artificial intelligence bubble inevitably bursts is, according to a provocative thread on /g/, a comforting delusion. Far from flooding the secondary market, the cards are allegedly destined for the smelter, consigned to be melted down and recycled into the next generation of silicon. Anons have fractured into opposing camps: those who insist that Nvidia hardware retains residual resale value, and those who contend that once hyperscale datacentres cease their voracious procurement, the enthusiast market will be left with depreciating inventory of dubious utility. The broader anxiety lurking beneath the discourse concerns the engineers themselves, whose livelihoods appear increasingly tethered to a single, possibly transient, technological paradigm.

clips.text_en_c2: The question surfaced on /a/ with genuine curiosity: does the board harbour affection for anime and manga of the sixties and seventies, an era the original poster contends produced work of a sophistication that Hanna-Barbera never approached? The thread laments the regrettable paucity of translations, observing that seminal works by towering mangakas of that period remain inaccessible to Anglophone audiences, their brilliance dimmed by linguistic neglect. Respondents invoked the era's distinctive aesthetic economy, its willingness to trust silence and suggestion, qualities that contemporary productions, saturated with exposition, often forfeit. The discussion evoked the mythic early days of Gundam, the patient wonder of Miyazaki's formative shorts, and a broader nostalgia for an artistic moment that, however imperfect, possessed an unmistakable conviction of purpose.
